items.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Where Late Quaternary extinctions were severe, archaeological, climatic, and extinction signals are compressed into short intervals, which makes their causes difficult to infer. Southern Africa offers a longer view because most of its large mammals survived. We tested whether, over a quarter of a million years, the size composition of hunted prey shifted toward smaller species and whether the estimated contribution of fat-rich prey changed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We reconstructed large-mammal records from 28 southern African sites and analyzed 71 human-accumulated assemblages from South Africa and Lesotho. We used the number of identified specimens (NISP) and a parallel dataset of minimum numbers of individuals (MNI). For each assemblage, we estimated the share of prey biomass contributed by each body-size class, and we related mean prey mass to assemblage age on a logarithmic scale. We estimated the biomass share of putatively fat-rich taxa using a size-based proxy, not a direct measure of dietary fat. We also assessed whether coastal inundation could account for the observed trends.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Large prey declined substantially through time. On MNI, animals above 296 kg supplied 84–89% of prey biomass in the Middle and late Middle Stone Age but 53% in the Later Stone Age. The megaherbivore (&gt;1,000 kg) share fell from approximately half to 8%. For every tenfold decrease in age, mean prey mass fell by 41% on NISP and 55% on MNI. The biomass share of putatively fat-rich taxa declined less, stayed above half throughout, and fell mainly between the Middle and the Later Stone Age. Coastal inundation explains a late pulse of large prey at the Cape coast, but not the broader decline across regions and earlier periods.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Interpretation is limited because the Middle Stone Age sample is mostly coastal and the Later Stone Age sample mostly inland. The robust result is a long-term decline in the proportion of large prey among kills. Fat-directed hunting under the protein ceiling and human depletion of large prey remain compatible hypotheses. Availability-referenced null models, mortality profiles, and genomic population histories can test them.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Due to their rapid reproductive cycles and short generation times, small mammals—particularly rodents and shrews—are widely used as bioindicators in ecological studies. While traditional live trapping provides detailed demographic data for such monitoring, it is labour‐intensive and subject to sampling bias. In contrast, owl pellet analysis presents a non‐invasive and cost‐effective alternative for evaluating small mammal community structure over broad spatial and temporal scales, though potential prey preferences should be considered. This study evaluates the effectiveness of owl pellet analysis in comparison to conventional trapping methods for monitoring small mammal communities. We synthesised data from 26 published studies and additional unpublished field reports, comprising a uniquely robust dataset of 40 systematically processed case studies across seven countries in Central Europe, a biogeographically coherent region. In all cases, trapping and pellet collection were carried out at the same locations and during the same periods, allowing for an exceptional level of methodological consistency. Results reveal that owl pellet analysis detects higher species diversity and provides a more efficient, non‐invasive means of monitoring small mammal assemblages over larger spatial and temporal scales. However, prey preferences and hunting behaviour of owls introduce biases, often overrepresenting abundant prey such as the common vole,
                    <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">
                      <jats:italic>Microtus arvalis</jats:italic>
                    </jats:styled-content>
                    and underrepresenting species associated with specific habitats or microclimates. These biases have significant implications for biodiversity assessments and paleoenvironmental reconstructions, where accurate community composition is essential. Our findings indicate that while owl pellet analysis is a valuable tool for ecological monitoring, careful consideration of predator selectivity is necessary to accurately interpret the results. Further research into owl hunting ecology is recommended to refine the application of this method in biodiversity studies and paleoecology.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Mesoamerican seasonally dry tropical forests (SDTFs) are floristically differentiated, spatially discontinuous and affected by Quaternary climatic change; yet, effects on long‐term suitability, refugial persistence and environmental connectivity remain unresolved. We assessed whether climatic oscillations over the last 800 ka altered the extent and connectivity of suitable SDTF areas more strongly than core position (areas of high climatic suitability). Climatic suitability was modelled for 103 woody plant species from 25 families and projected at 1‐ka intervals. Palaeoclimatic suitability dynamics, candidate refugia and connectivity were evaluated using continuous and binary multispecies consensus models. Maximum binary overlap remained high (89–94 models) across 22 representative palaeoclimatic time slices, while the main high‐suitability core persisted along the Pacific slope of western and southern Mexico. The Yucatán Peninsula and northern Central America showed temporal variation in suitability and continuity. Seven candidate refugial nuclei were identified, six forming a discontinuous Pacific chain and one in north‐eastern Yucatán. Connectivity analyses identified five sectors of potential environmental connectivity, the largest spanning the Balsas Basin–southern Mexico. No connection was detected between the Pacific and Gulf slopes, and northern Central America remained disconnected from Mexico. Quaternary climatic oscillations reconfigured the extent and spatial continuity of suitable environments while preserving persistent high‐suitability cores.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The mammalian rostrum has multiple functions including serving as the upper jaw, supporting olfactory sensory structures, conditioning inspired air, and—for some mammals—transmitting sound. Several groups of bats independently evolved bony inflations on the dorsolateral surfaces of their rostra. In rhinolophoid bats, rostral inflations are associated with nasal emission of echolocation calls, but their function in oral emitting bats (family Emballonuridae) is not well understood. Here, we combine μCT, diceCT, and histological methods to describe and quantify nasal fossa morphology of emballonurid bats in a comparative sample of 24 species overall, including 23 in the quantitative CT sample. Our goals are to (1) describe and quantify paranasal recess morphology, (2) explore scaling of paranasal recess size with body, skull, main nasal chamber, and turbinal size, (3) elucidate potential functions of rostral inflations in emballonurids, and (4) understand how nasal fossa morphology is related to presence of socially important glands and odor storing sacs in Emballonuridae. We report surprising diversity, clade‐specific traits, and several novelties in paranasal recess size and location among emballonurids. The combined volume of the paranasal recesses and main nasal chamber was more strongly correlated with peak echolocation call frequency used during foraging than with skull size. Some emballonurid species possess a well‐developed lateral nasal gland in the lateral recess. Other emballonurids have inflated, air‐filled paranasal recesses lined with thin, avascular mucosa, similar to those of nasal emitters with rostral inflations. We also observed turbinal traits reminiscent of those in nasal emitting Rhinolophidae. Proportionally large paranasal recesses are associated with reduced size and turbinal elements in emballonurid bats, except possibly in species that exhibit complex mating displays using perfume storing sacs in their wing membranes. Together, our results suggest that paranasal recesses could play a role in modifying echolocation calls in Emballonuridae, as they are hypothesized to do in nasophonating bats. However, the potential acoustic function of paranasal recesses remains to be experimentally elucidated in bats.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The expansion of the Linearbandkeramik (LBK; ca. 5400–4950 BCE) represents one of the most significant episodes of prehistoric population movement during the Neolithisation of Europe. Although migration is widely accepted as the principal mechanism of this expansion, the roles of ecological adaptation, population pressure and environmental constraints remain debated. We investigate diachronic changes in LBK settlement suitability using the human existence potential (HEP) approach, a species distribution modelling framework, applied to archaeological settlement data from the earliest (eLBK) and full LBK. HEP models were generated using two independent palaeoclimatic reconstructions (PaleoClim and CHELSA) combined with a soil quality index (SQI). Across all model variants, the environmental structure associated with persistent LBK settlement remained remarkably stable through time. Although the environmental envelope and geographical distribution expanded, many landscapes incorporated during later phases already exhibited high suitability in the eLBK models. The results provide little support for repeated large‐scale ecological adaptation or for population pressure and limits of carrying capacity as primary drivers of dispersal. Instead, they indicate considerable environmental flexibility from the outset and suggest that environmental suitability structured, but did not determine, the expansion of the LBK.</jats:p>
